utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-8-PT. The Prosecutor versus Dusko Sikirica, Dragan Kolundzija, and Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If it please the Court, Dirk Ryneveld, along with my co-counsel Daryl Mundis, for the Prosecution. Prepared to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my name is Veselih Londrovic and I am representing Dusko Sikirica in this case, together with my learned colleague Mr. Michael Greaves, who is also representing Dusko Sikirica in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my name is Vladimir Petrovic, I am a lawyer from Belgrade, and I am representing the interests of the accused Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Dusan Vucicevic on behalf of Dragan Kolundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The first matter that I have to deal with is this: The trial was listed for the 22nd of January. The Trial Chamber, for organisational reasons, can no longer hear the case on that date. We cannot give you another date, but I hope it will be early in March. That means this: That what had been listed as a pre-trial conference inevitably cannot be one because another conference will be required before the date of trial. The position is this, that we will fix another date before the end of this hearing. But there are matters which we can usefully deal with today to get the trial as ready as can be before trial. We have received the various briefs. We have also received the indictment. I mean the attachments to the indictment and an amended draft to that. It may be convenient to start with any matters connected with the indictment. Mr. Ryneveld, you've produced your attachment, as I say, and we've had today an amendment to it or an addition to it. As far as you're concerned, is the matter ready for trial as far as the indictment goes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Subject to this Trial Chamber's ruling on my friend's motion and our response and, as you know, we have just today filed a document which sets out the, shall we say, the culmination of what occurred on the 23rd of June when counsel orally indicated that there would be a modification to the indictment. We have set all that out and I have had discussions with my learned friend for Mr. Dosen and, as I understand it, he is content with the proposed amendment that we have proposed, or the amendment to the attachment. So to indicate to Your Honours directly, the answer is yes but for one issue. My friend has already raised with me that in paragraph 42 of the indictment against all seven, i.e., the indictment upon which we agreed last day that we would be proceeding, there is also reference in that paragraph 42 on page 12, reference to including the acts described in paragraphs 43 to 50 below. Now, you will note that in our response motion seeking leave to amend the attachment today, we have referred to paragraph 45 only as it relates to Mr. Dosen with regard to what is contained in paragraph 39 of the indictment. We did not make an application to amend the attachment or the indictment in regard to paragraph 42 because it charges all the other accused that are listed there. What we do want to indicate for the record, and I understand my friend is content with this, we want to say for the record that as it concerns Damir Dosen, the Prosecution is alleging only those acts under paragraph 42 described in paragraph 45, not 43 to 50 below. With respect to the others, i.e., Sikirica, Fustar, and Kolundzija, the paragraphs 43 to 50 apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Anything the Defence want to say about that, that matter having been clarified?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm satisfied with the submission that has been made by my learned colleague from the Prosecution, and the problem which was raised some time ago in my motion has been completely solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Turning to the pre-trial briefs which have been submitted and the Defence of Mr. Sikirica, there is a reference to a notice of alibi to be produced by Mr. Sikirica. Is that still relied on and, if so, when is the notice to be produced? We may have to make a ruling as far as that's concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The answer to Your Honour's first question is yes, and as soon as possible, although at the present time I don't know precisely when we can produce such a document. I'm sorry to be a bit vague at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. 1st of February we have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To concentrate minds. And the Prosecution should have the information in time to make inquiries, if they want, before trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as the brief for Mr. Kolundzija is concerned, there's reference at one stage to diminished responsibility under notice. Mr. Vucicevic, is diminished responsibility still to be relied on or not? If it is, we'll have to have a notice in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It will be relied on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. Any reason why we shouldn't have a notice in relation to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I have given the notice of the alibi -- of the diminished mental capacity of the accused shortly after he was examined by a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that was filed with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm told it has been, so there's no difficulty about that. Thank you. Turning to the witnesses. Mr. Ryneveld, have we got a definitive list of witnesses now on whom you're going to rely?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. It's our position that we do. Both contained in our 65 ter witness list and in our subsequent motion for additional protected measures we have listed, that is the box, as it were, containing the entire list of witnesses of which we are aware at the moment, and that is the list that has been suggested and that is the list that we'll be proceeding with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And as far as timing is concerned, we would encourage you not to call a great deal of oral evidence about background events and try to deal with those as much as possible by way of written documents and other statements, any other form of evidence, at least to be considered as a way of producing the background, and concentrate on the core issues, which is, of course, the culpability of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That is our intention, yes, Your Honour. Leading to another issue about admissions, hopefully, we have been trying to attend to some of those matters with my friends. Unfortunately, to date we have not been particularly successful in hammering out any additional admissions. Part of the difficulty is it takes three counsel and the Prosecution to agree on all matters, otherwise, we still have to lead evidence where one of the counsel do not agree. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are all here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We met yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You met yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We've had correspondence. We've had previous meetings. It is not for a lack of attempt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I'm sure that's right, but there is the opportunity which these conferences provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it proposed that you should meet again to try to agree on some facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I would encourage my friends to meet with us yet again to see whether perhaps once we are able to distill what is contained in those pre-trial briefs, for example, that there may be some common ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, of course, we would say to the Defence that we encourage you to meet with the Prosecution and secure common ground. It is pointless to have a trial which is going to be over matters which, in the event, turn out not to be in dispute. And it's really the duty of counsel to try to achieve areas of common ground before the trial begins. In this case, there will be an extra six weeks or so in which to do it. Mr. Ryneveld, as far as the witnesses are concerned, it's been noted that at least two of them, Mr. Vulliamy and a Mr. Selak have given evidence in other cases. Is there any reason why transcripts should not be served in their case and used?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, we are contemplating doing that with respect to as many witnesses as possible and not necessarily only Mr. Vulliamy or Osman Selak. Witness Greve is, perhaps, also a candidate, having testified before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There are perhaps others. There are other witnesses who have testified in other proceedings, transcripts have been provided, and those are among those areas where I'm hoping to find some fertile ground for shortening the proceedings in consultation with my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that matter should be expedited for this reason, that if the transcripts cannot be agreed and there are issues to be decided, then the Trial Chamber should decide them, if necessary, and if possible, before the trial so that it's known whether it's necessary to call the witnesses or not. There's no reason why the Trial Chamber shouldn't, at an appropriate time, decide on the admissibility of the transcripts. We now have experience, of course, of dealing with that and it's been dealt with in a number of cases. While you are on your feet, the issue of experts arises to deal with exhumations and the like. Are you proposing to call experts of that sort?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We do have some experts on our list with respect to exhumations and, again, that is another area which we have tried to seek some unanimity. Again, I'm not ruling out the possibility that that might not be dealt with by agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Isn't that a matter for agreement? Presumably the issue is it may well be the numbers involved in these various graves. I don't know whether identity could possibly be an issue or not but it would seem to be an area where much evidence is not necessary, particularly repetitious evidence. Turning to the Defence, first of all, the issue of transcripts is one which, if possible, you should look at to see if it's possible to have transcripts read. If it's not, we will rule on whether the transcripts should be admitted or not. I can tell you now that what we look at is to see what the issues raised are, that is, whether cross-examination in this particular case of the witness is necessary for any reason as opposed to the cross-examination which occurred in the earlier case which may well have covered all the relevant issues. In particular, if there is evidence about one of the accused which it's proposed to give by way of transcript, we would look at that very closely to see whether cross-examination is necessary or not. But if it's dealing with background issues, matters of that sort, why, then we may well be inclined to admit a transcript. So it would be very much, if you are considering this, it would be very much the nature of the evidence as opposed to whether there is some general principle of giving evidence orally or not. Likewise, as far as the exhumation evidence is concerned and the evidence of any experts, that would appear to be a matter which is really susceptible of agreement between the parties without a great deal of evidence being given about it. I hope it will be possible to reach agreement. We have to consider the question of time. It's a matter which has been discussed and the Prosecution, I think, have indicated a preference for a limitation by way of time as opposed to a limitation by way of a number of witnesses. That is something which we, at the moment, wouldn't decide on, but given the pressures that there are on the Tribunal in terms of time in which cases are taking, we would be keen to be looking at that possibility and maybe setting a time limit. Could I turn next -- we can return to any other matters anybody wants to raise, but I am dealing with some matters generally. The question of exhibits. As far as I understand the position, the Prosecution have not yet filed a list of the exhibits, or am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My recollection, Your Honour, is that we have had three binders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- of documents already admitted on a previous motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And we have outstanding before you an application for admission of two more binders under additional requests for admission of documentary evidence, which we filed on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's it. My understanding is that my learned friends, and I think -- at least, I'm not sure whether all of them, but we did have a discussion about this and my understanding was that they took no objection to those additional matters also being filed on the same basis as the others were; that if -- that they wouldn't contest the issue of authenticity or admissibility, but if there was a particular challenge to a document, it would be dealt with during -- during the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But I don't think -- I know that my learned friends Londrovic and Mr. Petrovic had that discussion with us. Mr. Vucicevic was ill at the time so this is something I haven't been able to address with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps the convenient way is, rather than discussing it here, is if Mr. Vucicevic and yourself could meet to discuss that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. That's it with respect to exhibits. This is not the kind of case where, other than the documents that we've now in, a complete set of five binders, three already in and two pending. We don't anticipate any further exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the final matter I want to raise is the matter of outstanding motions, and we have a motion from Mr. Vucicevic in relation to the disclosure of materials by the United Nations. You ask for a subpoena directed to them. Have you, Mr. Vucicevic, approached the United Nations to see if they would give you the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought that would be a futile step because in June of 1998, when I cross-examined Witness Greve, that I included the transcript of that colloquy, she had difficulties, having been an expert that suggested establishment, empowerment of this Court, she had extreme difficulty in obtaining the names of the officers in their location. With that in mind, Your Honour, I thought the only purview would be to get a subpoena from this body to pursue this matter. I understand it was your directions to Defence counsel when we faced the decision on the similar motion in May of 1998, prior -- in Kovacevic's pre-trial, but I believe that was cleared up by Witness Greve's detailed explanation on how she couldn't get those documents, how she couldn't get the names of the officers, how she couldn't get any cooperation from the military -- office of the military observers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, we have other experience, not in this case but in other cases, and in any event, the procedure is to ask the body that you want the documents from to see what sort of a response you get. Now, our order is then that you ask -- make a request of the United Nations for the documents, specifying what documents you want. If the response is not satisfactory to you, then you could raise the matter with us again and at least we'll know what the response of the United Nations is and we can take the matter forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I do thank you for your recommendation and basically the essence of the order, Your Honour, but the time constraints that we are facing might preclude any meaningful result on this one. And I have been dealing with the United Nations subsequently to the trial that I mentioned already, on some other issues, and I have found an extremely difficult time to get any responses or information from the body. So, you know, it would be quite difficult even were to drag those questions because that the office of the military observers in Bosnia has been defunct now for four or five years. I thought that some recommendations from the Court or directions from the Court would expedite the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: See how you get on and you can report back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ryneveld, I have a question for you concerning the attachment that the Trial Chamber requested you to submit with the indictment, the amended indictment. As regards Mr. Sikirica, I should like to know the following: The genocide charge against Mr. Sikirica, does it not have an impact onto other accused in this case? You allege that their acts would constitute genocide, for which Mr. Sikirica would be responsible in accordance with the provision regarding the individual responsibility, Article 7(3) of the Statute. So I would like to know whether in the attachment that you have submitted upon the request of the Chamber the fact of mentioning Mr. Dosen and Mr. Kolundzija as co-perpetrators or accomplices, does that fact not have an implication on the other accused regarding these particular charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry for the delay. I was just discussing with my colleague. As I understand Your Honour's question does it not impact, the difficulty, as I understand it, is it is only Mr. Sikirica that is charged with genocide and not the other two. You can have, as I understand it, circumstances whereby his 7(3) responsibility includes the acts of others who may not be necessarily charged with that conduct but he is being charged with that conduct. We have not, through our attachment, attempted to expand upon the charges against Dosen or Sikirica or others because it's Sikirica only that stands charged with genocide. I don't know whether I've answered your question how does it impact. It is part of the overall narrative to explain how it is we say that Mr. Sikirica's 7(3) responsibility for genocide is accomplished through the means of others under his command but -- and although I suppose in an academic or technical way had we chosen, we could have chosen to charge others with genocide, but in this particular case it was only Mr. Sikirica that is charged. So the impact must be restricted by the charge itself and not the evidentiary basis upon which others might be found connected. That's my attempt at answering Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm reminded that there is an outstanding motion for protective measures filed by the Prosecution on the 10th of November to which the Defence are due to reply by the 24th of November. At the moment, I don't think there's any objection been raised. Perhaps the Defence can assist us. If there is no objection to this most, then it will be granted. Can you assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we discussed this yesterday at the meeting with the Prosecution. My learned friend Mr. Londrovic indicated then that we had no objection to the order being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have anything to add. This is our position as well. So we do not have any objection to these motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: No objection on behalf of Mr. Kolundzija, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Granted. One final matter remains on this before we go into closed session, unless the parties want to raise anything, but the question arises about fixing another date for another conference. Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If this is our opportunity to raise other matters, and I don't mean to be presumptuous, but we did have some discussions about perhaps procedural matters which counsel had thought perhaps asking for the Court's direction about concerning conduct of the trial itself. One of those issues is -- has to do with the issue of witnesses who have testified in other proceedings and the provision of that information to Defence counsel for these accused in the most economical way rather than send all these transcripts for translation purposes, we wondered whether perhaps the Court might agree that a provision of a videotape in B/C/S or an audiotape, as Mr. Londrovic would prefer, could be provided to them in addition to the transcript, which is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we've done that in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So on their behalf, I'm making that request. Thank you. There are some other matters, procedural issues at trial. My understanding of the jurisprudence in this particular jurisdiction is that there is a practice that there will be no contact with the witness by any counsel once they have basically taken the solemn declaration. There are, from time to time, exceptions, urgent situations where counsel ask leave of the Court for permission for counsel to make that communication, and usually that is done in the presence of other counsel. So in some exigent circumstances, we wondered whether perhaps the Court might entertain the possibility, or by agreement of counsel, for example, over a weekend. So if all counsel agreed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: These are just some things we were trying to iron out in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The rule is there should be no contact. Obviously, things arise which means that there has to be contact. If that is the position, then the leave of the Trial Chamber which made the order should be sought. In an extraordinary case where the Trial Chamber wasn't sitting, then the matter -- and there was contact, the matter would have to be brought to the attention of the Trial Chamber immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The final issue, I think, may have now been rendered moot by virtue of the fact that you are discussing a different trial date, but one of the issues that we did want to raise was perhaps a sitting schedule so that we would be in contact with victim witness people in preparation for January 22nd. But that has been rendered moot and those are the issues I wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As soon as there is a date, there would be a schedule of the sitting and, in fact, what I would anticipate is that we would, during the pre-trial conference, announce what the schedule will be. Is there anything that Defence counsel want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. I confirm we had a conversation yesterday about contact with witnesses. Your Honour will know that in my jurisdiction, as in Your Honour's jurisdiction, sometimes these matters can be dealt with by agreement of counsel without reference to the Trial Chamber or to the Trial Judge. I don't know whether Your Honour would feel that it's appropriate to trust us to sort matters out as between counsel if something arises. For example, the witness wants to do something in particular which doesn't need to trouble the Trial Chamber, a matter of -- that has to be dealt with between counsel but doesn't need to be dealt with on the basis of assembling a full Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are no longer in the jurisdiction with which we are familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, of course. But I'm just wondering whether -- it may be that we can frame an order that gives us certain latitude that doesn't necessarily have to involve Your Honours. That's what I'm trying to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If a formulation can be made which is satisfactory, but remember that we are three, we are sitting as a Trial Chamber, and therefore normally anything should come to us but, of course, we'll consider a formulation before the trial begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May I suggest then that, between Defence and Prosecution, we can sit down and try to work out a sensible form of words for presentation to the Trial Chamber and, if the Trial Chamber likes it, it can adopt it or adapt it as it so chooses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If there are no other matters to be dealt with in open court, it leaves the question of a date, and I'm going to ask for a calendar, please. Unless there are any submissions. Do counsel have any submissions about a suitable date? As I say, we are looking to a start date for the trial but it's not a matter that is within our hands at the moment. But we are looking for one or anticipating one in early March, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The convenient time which is suggested is Monday, the 5th of February at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: For the pre-trial conference? I'm sorry, the 5th of February --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is Monday, the 5th of February for the next conference. Whether it's the pre-trial conference or not will depend whether or not we can start the trial. Very well, we'll go into closed session to deal with any other matters.

procedural_notes.text: ---  Whereupon the Status Conference was adjourned
